headline: Scientists Find a Way to Make French Fries Healthier Without Losing the Crunch
meta_description: Researchers at University of Illinois combine microwave and conventional frying to reduce oil absorption in French fries while keeping them crispy.
summary_short: A new cooking method blends microwave heating with traditional frying to cut oil absorption and cooking time while preserving the crispy texture people love.
body:
Researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign have discovered that combining microwave energy with conventional frying could produce healthier French fries without sacrificing the crispy exterior and satisfying texture that consumers crave. The breakthrough addresses a fundamental problem: fried foods absorb large amounts of oil during cooking, increasing fat and calorie content and contributing to obesity and hypertension. By harnessing microwave energy to keep oil out while using conventional frying to create crunch, scientists believe they can shorten cooking time, limit oil uptake, and still deliver the flavor-rich fries people expect. The key lies in understanding pressure inside the potato. As potatoes cook, water turns to vapor and escapes, creating empty spaces where negative pressure can draw oil into the food—a process that accounts for as much as 90 percent of frying. Microwave energy heats water molecules throughout the potato rather than from the surface inward, generating more vapor and maintaining positive pressure inside, which keeps oil out.

Principal investigator Pawan Singh Takhar, a professor of food engineering in the Department of Food Science and Human Nutrition, explained the physics simply: "When there is positive pressure, the oil stays out. But if there is negative pressure, the oil starts moving in." Working with collaborators at Washington State University, who had developed a specialized microwave fryer operating at different frequencies, the team tested their approach by blanching, salting, and frying potato strips in soybean oil heated to 180 degrees Celsius. Measurements tracked temperature, pressure, moisture, and oil content throughout cooking.

While microwave frying alone produced soggy results, the hybrid method showed promise. When combined with conventional frying, microwave energy reduced total cooking time and lowered oil absorption. The research, detailed in mathematical models and laboratory experiments, offers a practical pathway toward making one of the world's favorite comfort foods both healthier and faster to prepare.
quick_facts: University of Illinois researchers combine microwave and conventional frying methods
Microwave frying reduces oil absorption while keeping fries crispy
Potato cooking time and fat content both decrease with hybrid method
Up to 90% of oil absorption occurs under negative pressure inside food
Oil heated to 180 degrees Celsius during testing
